definition.text: Insurance is protection from financial loss: for a fee, one party promises to pay another if a particular loss, damage or injury happens.

facts.text: It is a form of risk management, used mainly to guard against a loss that may or may not happen.
The buyer accepts a certain, known and fairly small loss, the premium, in exchange for the insurer's promise to pay if a covered loss occurs.
A deductible (or excess) is the amount the insured must pay out of pocket before the insurer pays a claim.
Insurance transfers the financial burden of a chance event to a bigger entity; it does not lower the chance that the event happens.
Needing an insurable interest, a real stake in the loss, is what separates insurance from gambling.
Chinese and Indian traders spread risk as early as the 3rd and 2nd millennia BC; Chinese merchants split cargo across many boats so one capsizing lost little.
Economists and consumer advocates in the United States generally see insurance as worthwhile for rare, catastrophic losses but not for likely, small ones.
Insurance can help households and societies prepare for and soften catastrophes, but it can also raise fraud and careless behaviour.

definition.text: Risk pooling is gathering money from many insured people or firms so that it can pay the losses that only some of them will suffer.

facts.text: Each member is protected for a fee, and the fee depends on how often and how badly the insured event tends to happen.
Because policies cover members of large classes, insurers can rely on the law of large numbers, under which predicted losses come close to actual losses.
Instead of joining a pool, a person or firm can self-insure by saving money for possible future losses.
Some communities, including the Amish and some Muslim groups, rely on mutual support from their community when disaster strikes rather than on insurance contracts.

definition.text: Insurability is the set of features a risk must have for private companies to be able to insure it.

facts.text: An insurable loss should be definite in time, place and cause, accidental rather than in the insured's control, and large enough to matter to the buyer.
Both the probability of loss and its cost must be at least estimable, and the premium must stay affordable relative to the cover.
Losses should ideally be independent and not catastrophic, so they do not all strike at once and bankrupt the insurer.
Limited capital constrains how much earthquake insurance, and wind insurance in hurricane zones, insurers can sell.

definition.text: An insurance premium is the price charged for cover, set to cover expected claims, costs and profit, minus what the insurer earns by investing it.

facts.text: Setting premiums, called ratemaking, is actuarial work that uses statistics and probability to estimate future claims for a given risk.
Insurers bring historical loss data to present value and compare it with premiums collected to judge whether rates are adequate.
Float is money collected as premiums but not yet paid out in claims; insurers invest it and earn income on it until claims are paid.
US property and casualty insurers lost $142.3 billion on underwriting in the five years ending 2003 but made $68.4 billion overall thanks to float.

definition.text: Reinsurance is insurance for insurance companies: another insurer agrees to carry part of a risk that the first insurer finds too large.

facts.text: The reinsurance market is dominated by a few large companies with huge reserves.
Single properties worth more than any one insurer's capital limit are shared among several insurers or syndicated into the reinsurance market.

definition.text: Property insurance protects against risks to property such as fire, theft or weather, and includes special forms for floods, earthquakes and crops.

facts.text: Crop insurance helps farmers manage losses from weather, hail, drought, frost, pests or disease.
Index-based insurance pays farmers when a modelled climate trigger, linked to a high chance of large crop loss, is exceeded and harvest losses occur.
Many US insurers do not offer flood insurance in some regions, so the federal National Flood Insurance Program acts as insurer of last resort.
